巴烏主要出現在現代中國傳統樂器合奏作品中，也常作為獨奏樂器使用，並見於電影配樂與: The bawu appears mainly in modern ensemble works for Chinese traditional instruments, and it is often used as a solo instrument; it also appears in film scores and pop recordings. In southwest China it is closely tied to the music of the Miao, Yi and Hani peoples; in Thailand a similar free-reed instrument of the Miao can be used in the piphat ensemble. In recent years European players such as Rohan Leach, Raphael De Cock, Seán Mac Erlaine and Herman Witkam have brought it into new music practice, and Guo Yue has gone on using it in his recordings.
巴烏可能起源於中國西南雲南，與苗族、彝族、哈尼族等西南少數民族文化密切相關，後成: The bawu probably originated in Yunnan in southwest China and is closely tied to the cultures of the Miao, Yi, Hani and other minority peoples of the southwest; it later became a standard instrument in traditional ensembles across China and in modern Chinese works. It is often played solo and also appears in film scores and pop recordings; outside China it has in recent years been taken up by European composers and players, and Guo Yue, who lives in Britain, has long promoted it and plays it on his recordings. People in Taiwan also use instruments of this kind at Lunar New Year. Recently some makers have thickened and lengthened the body and added keys to increase the volume and improve intonation, which gives two octaves; in the Yi areas of the Red River, vertically blown and double-pipe bawu are also popular.
巴烏橫持，吹孔側向，口含吹孔但嘴唇不接觸簧片。發聲時可吸氣或呼氣，惟吸氣時高音不: The bawu is held horizontally with the blow hole at the side; you put the hole to your mouth but your lips do not touch the reed. You can sound it by breathing in or out, though the upper register is hard to sound on the intake and some low notes are less true. A beginner can first cover the eight finger holes, seven in front and one behind, and practise steady airflow and a close seal on the holes, then add decorations such as the bent note.
巴烏管身以竹製成，一端由天然竹節封閉；另有資料記為竹製或木製。發聲體為簧片，來源: The body of the bawu is of bamboo, closed at one end by a natural node; other sources record it as bamboo or wood. The sounding body is a reed, recorded in the source as bronze or copper and described as a long, narrow isosceles triangle cut in a thin metal plate. Round the blow hole is a low mouthpiece of plastic or bone. The common two-piece instrument is joined with a metal tenon; keyed versions usually do not use natural bamboo. The materials of other parts are not stated in the source.
巴烏音色純淨，近似單簧管；低音區泛音豐富，最低泛音強度接近基音，帶有簧片共鳴的嗡: The bawu's timbre is pure and close to the clarinet's. In the low register the overtones are rich, the lowest overtone nearly as strong as the fundamental, which gives the buzz of a reed resonance rather like a harmonica; in the upper register the even overtones are weak and the odd ones dominate, so the timbre turns clarinet-like. Playing often uses ornaments, especially the bent note. The sound comes from a single free reed of copper or bronze, and the mouth does not touch the reed; like the sheng it can be blown or drawn, but on the intake the upper register is hard to sound and some low notes go out of tune. The usual range is about an eleventh, from B to E in the key of G; keys extend it upward or in both directions, and a thickened, lengthened body can give two octaves. The volume is usually small, and keys and a thicker, longer body can increase it.
巴烏（Bawu）是中國氣鳴自由簧樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號412: The bawu is a Chinese free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.131. The body is of bamboo or wood, about 27 cm long, with eight finger holes, seven in front and one behind; a blow hole opens at the side near one end, and inside sits a pointed-tongue reed of copper, which sounds when you blow with the hole at your mouth. It is common in Yi, Miao, Hani and other cultures, and it is used to accompany dance and narrative singing, for solos, in film scores and on pop recordings, and on occasions such as Lunar New Year.
